justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term trajectory with modest upward drift over longer horizons. For the 1-day estimate of 812, I was anchoring closely to what appeared to be the prevailing market level at the time of the forecast, assuming continuity of recent momentum with minimal overnight disruption. The 1-week estimate of 818 incorporates a slight positive drift, reflecting a baseline assumption that the underlying trend remains constructive without any major catalysts expected to reverse it. The 1-month estimate of 825 extends that modest drift further, essentially projecting a slow grind higher consistent with a low-volatility, mean-reverting environment punctuated by incremental gains.

Confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the range of 789 to 835 is relatively tight because the dominant sources of noise — intraday volatility, overnight gaps — are reasonably well-characterized. By one week, the interval widens to capture earnings releases, macroeconomic data prints, and sentiment shifts that could materially move the market in either direction. At one month, the range of 720 to 930 is quite wide because monetary policy signals, geopolitical developments, and liquidity conditions can interact in nonlinear ways that are genuinely hard to anticipate.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside even these wider intervals include a sudden central bank policy surprise — for instance, an emergency rate decision or unexpected forward guidance shift — which could compress or spike the asset sharply beyond the stated bounds. A significant geopolitical shock, credit event, or systemic liquidity disruption could easily breach the lower end of the monthly interval. On the upside, an unexpected resolution of a major macro overhang or a large coordinated policy stimulus could push prices well above 930. These tail risks are real but were judged low-probability at the time of the forecast, which is why they sit outside rather than inside the 90% confidence intervals.

It is also worth noting that the intervals themselves carry model uncertainty — the true coverage of these ranges depends heavily on distributional assumptions about returns, and in practice financial markets exhibit fat tails that make 90% intervals harder to achieve than they appear. Readers should treat the bounds as indicative of my uncertainty rather than as precise probabilistic guarantees.
